passages.happening:
Joseph gives his steward an order. Fill the men's sacks with food and put each man's silver back. “Put my cup, the silver one, in the mouth of the youngest one's sack” (verse 2).

At daybreak the brothers leave. Before they have gone far, Joseph sends the steward after them to ask, “Why have you repaid good with evil?” (verse 4). “Is this not the cup my master drinks from and uses for divination? What you have done is wicked!” (verse 5).

The brothers are shocked. “Your servants could not possibly do such a thing” (verse 7). They make a rash promise: “If any of your servants is found to have it, he must die, and the rest will become slaves of my lord” (verse 9). The steward says only the one with the cup will be a slave (verse 10).

He searches from the oldest to the youngest, “and the cup was found in Benjamin's sack” (verse 12). “Then they all tore their clothes, loaded their donkeys, and returned to the city” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
A silver cup was a luxury in an Egyptian lord's house. Stealing from such a house was a grave crime. The Laws of Hammurabi, from Babylon about 1754 BC, punished theft of temple or palace property by death. So the brothers' promise was not just talk. It named the kind of penalty such a theft could bring. The steward's answer is milder.

The search is told slowly on purpose. The steward begins with the oldest. Sack after sack is opened. The reader knows where the cup is. The brothers do not. Only at the very last sack is it found.

Now comes the real test. The steward has said the rest can go free. The brothers could walk home with their grain and leave Benjamin behind as a slave. Twenty years ago they left a son of Rachel in a pit and sold him. What will they do now?

They tear their clothes, the sign of grief and shock. The last time clothes were torn in this story, Reuben and Jacob tore theirs over Joseph (37:29, 34). Now every brother tears his clothes over Benjamin. And every one of them turns back.
passages.later:
Israel's later law forbids divination. “You must not practice divination or sorcery” (Leviticus 19:26). “Let no one be found among you who sacrifices his son or daughter in the fire, practices divination or conjury, interprets omens, practices sorcery” (Deuteronomy 18:10).

The steward's charge, repaying ‘good with evil’, uses the same pair of words Joseph will use at the end of the story (Genesis 50:20).
passages.hard:
Did Joseph practise divination? Divination means trying to learn secret things or the future by reading signs. Babylonian omen texts describe one way of doing it with a cup: watching the shapes that drops of oil made on water.

What the text says is narrow. The steward is told to say that this is the cup his master ‘uses for divination’ (verse 5), and Joseph says he ‘can surely divine the truth’ (verse 15). Both lines are spoken inside the trick, by a man playing the part of an Egyptian lord. The narrator never tells us that Joseph used the cup in this way.

Readers take this in three main ways. Some think it is only part of Joseph's disguise, since nowhere else does Joseph seek omens, and he insists that the meaning of dreams belongs to God (40:8; 41:16). Others think Joseph, living in Egypt long before the law was given, may have kept such a cup as Egyptian officials did, and Genesis simply reports it. A third view points to the irony: Joseph needs no cup to know the truth about these men. He knows exactly who they are.

These notes do not claim more than the text says. And the trap itself is a deception, as Genesis plainly shows. Some readers see it as a hard but needed test on the way to real peace. Others think Genesis, which reports many deceptions without praising them, shows Joseph's methods as mixed, even while God works through them.
passages.asks: The brothers were offered an easy way home without Benjamin, and none of them took it. Ask whether there is a moment coming where you could save yourself by leaving someone else to pay. Then ask what kind of person you have been becoming, so that you will be ready for it.

passages.t: ‘God has exposed the iniquity of your servants’
passages.happening:
“When Judah and his brothers arrived at Joseph's house, he was still there, and they fell to the ground before him” (verse 14).

“What is this deed you have done?” Joseph says. “Do you not know that a man like me can surely divine the truth?” (verse 15).

“What can we say to my lord?” Judah answers. “How can we plead? How can we justify ourselves? God has exposed the iniquity of your servants. We are now my lord's slaves” (verse 16).

Joseph says no. Only “The man who was found with the cup will be my slave. The rest of you may return to your father in peace” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Notice how the narrator names them now: ‘Judah and his brothers’. Judah has become the leader.

They fall to the ground before Joseph. Once more, his dream comes true.

Listen closely to Judah. He did not steal the cup. None of them did. Yet he does not argue. He says, ‘God has exposed the iniquity of your servants.’ Iniquity means guilt, wrongdoing. Judah knows he is innocent of this crime, and he knows he is not innocent. He reads the false charge as God bringing the old crime to light. He is speaking of the pit and the silver, though the Egyptian lord, he thinks, cannot know it.

And he says ‘we’. We are all slaves, he says, not only Benjamin. The brothers will not leave him alone.

Joseph presses one more time. ‘The rest of you may return to your father in peace.’ The door is open. They could go.
passages.later: Judah's words sound like the prayers of confession in the Psalms: “For I know my transgressions, and my sin is always before me” (Psalm 51:3). Jesus told of a tax collector who would not even lift up his eyes, but said, “God, have mercy on me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13).
passages.asks: Judah stopped defending himself and said that God had brought his guilt to light. Ask whether there is a time you were blamed for the wrong thing and knew you were guilty of something else. Then ask what God might be bringing into the open in your life.

passages.happening:
“Then Judah approached Joseph and said, ‘Sir, please let your servant speak personally to my lord’” (verse 18).

He tells the whole story again. The lord asked about their father and brother (verse 19). They told him of “an elderly father and a younger brother, the child of his old age” (verse 20). The lord demanded to see the boy. They warned that “If he were to leave, his father would die” (verse 22).

Then Judah repeats what his father said to them: “You know that my wife bore me two sons. When one of them was gone, I said: ‘Surely he has been torn to pieces.’ And I have not seen him since” (verses 27-28). “Now if you also take this one from me and harm comes to him, you will bring my gray hair down to Sheol in sorrow” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
This is one of the longest speeches in Genesis. Judah steps up to the most powerful man in Egypt. He is polite and humble. He calls Joseph ‘my lord’ and himself ‘your servant’. He even says Joseph is ‘equal to Pharaoh himself’ (verse 18).

He tells the story again, but with a new centre: the father. The word ‘father’ runs all through his speech. Judah is pleading for an old man's life.

Then comes the most painful line. Judah repeats his father's words: ‘my wife bore me two sons.’ Jacob had twelve sons by four women. But in his heart only Rachel was ‘my wife’, and only her two boys were truly his. Judah is Leah's son. He was not one of the two.

Twenty years ago, the brothers could not bear their father's favoritism. They hated Joseph for it and got rid of him. Now Judah repeats his father's favoritism out loud, without bitterness. He accepts it, for his father's sake.

And listen to how Judah speaks of Joseph: ‘Surely he has been torn to pieces.’ He is standing in front of Joseph as he says it. Joseph hears his brother tell, with sorrow, the lie they told their father.
passages.later:
When David's son Absalom died, David cried out, “O my son Absalom!” (2 Samuel 18:33). The Bible does not hide how deep a father's grief can go.

Later Scripture uses the same picture of one life bound up with another for the friendship of Jonathan and David: “the souls of Jonathan and David were knit together” (1 Samuel 18:1).
passages.asks: Judah accepted his father's unequal love without bitterness and pleaded for the old man's sake. Ask whether there is a hurt from a parent's favoritism that still shapes how you treat your family. Then ask whether love for someone else could be stronger than that hurt.

passages.t: ‘Let your servant stay here in place of the boy’
passages.happening:
Judah says that if he goes home without the boy, his father, “whose life is wrapped up in the boy's life” (verse 30), will die (verse 31).

“Indeed, your servant guaranteed the boy's safety to my father” (verse 32).

Then he makes his offer. “Now please let your servant stay here as my lord's slave in place of the boy. Let him return with his brothers” (verse 33).

“For how can I go back to my father without the boy? I could not bear to see the misery that would overwhelm him” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
This is the turning point of the whole Joseph story.

Remember Judah in chapter 37. It was Judah who said, ‘Come, let us sell him’ (37:27). He turned his brother into a slave for twenty shekels of silver. He watched his father's grief and said nothing.

Now Judah stands before the same brother, without knowing it, and asks to be made a slave himself, for life, so that the youngest son of Rachel can go home. The man who sold a brother into slavery offers to become a slave in a brother's place.

This is what Joseph has been waiting to see. Not words of regret only, but a changed man. The brothers have been given every chance to leave Benjamin behind. Judah will not.

Notice too what moves him. It is not fear for himself. ‘I could not bear to see the misery that would overwhelm him.’ The brother who once watched his father's grief without pity now cannot bear the thought of it.

The word for this is substitution: one person taking another's place, and bearing what the other would have borne.
passages.later:
Jesus was born of Judah's tribe. Revelation calls him “the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David” (Revelation 5:5). Many Christians read Judah's offer as a picture that points ahead to Christ, who gave himself in the place of others. Jesus said that he came “to give His life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45), and Peter writes that Christ suffered “the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God” (1 Peter 3:18).

The New Testament does not quote this chapter, so this is a reading, not a prophecy. And the likeness has a telling difference. Judah is a guilty man offering himself for an innocent brother. In the gospel, the innocent one gives himself for the guilty.

Jacob will later say of this son, “Judah, your brothers shall praise you” (Genesis 49:8).
passages.asks: The man who once sold his brother now offered himself in his brother's place. Ask whether you believe a person can truly change, including you. Then ask whose place you might be willing to take, and what it would cost.
